function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run manually) to get the repo ready for Docker, Kubernetes and CI/CD.  
All the files that need to be added are shown in full – just drop them into the appropriate locations and commit/push.

> **NOTE**  
> *The repo you’re working on is a simple Node.js “Hello‑World” app.  
> The Docker image will be built from the official Node LTS image, the Kubernetes manifests will expose the app on port 80, and the GitHub Actions workflow will build the image, run tests, push the image to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) and deploy it to a cluster.*

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the **root** of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Use the official Node.js LTS image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure and contains the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install of the exact versions in `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port 3000 (the default for many Node examples).

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes manifests

Create a directory `k8s/` in the repo root and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Two replicas of the pod are created.  
> * The service exposes the pods on port 80 inside the cluster, forwarding traffic to the container’s port 3000.  
> * The image name uses the GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`) – you’ll push the image there in the CI workflow.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    # Checkout the repo
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    # Set up Node.js
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    # Install dependencies
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    # Build Docker image
    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build -t nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
        echo "${{ secrets.GHCR_TOKEN }}" | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
        docker tag nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

    # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a KUBECONFIG secret)
    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          ./k8s/deployment.yaml
          ./k8s/service.yaml
        images: |
          ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        namespace: default
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `GHCR_TOKEN` – a GitHub Container Registry token with `write:packages` permission.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – the kubeconfig file for the cluster you want to deploy to (base64‑encoded).  
>   (If you’re not deploying automatically, you can skip the last job.)

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push lands, GitHub Actions will kick off, build the image, push it to GHCR, and deploy it to your cluster (if you have the `KUBECONFIG` secret set).

---

### Quick sanity check

After the workflow finishes, you can verify:

```bash
# Pull the image locally (optional)
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>

# Inspect the Kubernetes resources
kubectl get deployments,svc
```

That’s it! Your repo now contains everything needed for containerisation, Kubernetes deployment, and continuous integration. Happy coding!
